snippet: a tombstone in Egypt is dated Ramadan 29 AH
correction: a tombstone in Cyprus is dated Ramadan 29 AH
problem: The tombstone of 'Urwa b. Thabit dated Ramadan 29 AH (650 CE) is reported from Cyprus, not Egypt. The earliest dated Egyptian tombstone is a different one (Aswan, 31 AH).
old_html: a tombstone in Egypt is dated Ramadan 29 AH

snippet: show the same surah text in the first Islamic century
correction: show a text that is, in the portions preserved, very close to today's Quran. The Sana'a lower text does contain variants, which scholars debate
problem: The Sana'a palimpsest lower text contains many variants from the standard Uthmanic text (Sadeghi and Bergmann, Arabica 57, 2010), and the Birmingham folios are only a small portion. Saying they show "the same text" overstates it.
old_html: show the same surah text in the first Islamic century

snippet: Zayd ibn Thabit accepted a passage only if it was found in writing and confirmed by memorisers (Bukhari 4986)
correction: Zayd collected the Quran from written fragments and from memorisers (Bukhari 4986); later scholars such as Ibn Hajar explain that he required two witnesses for each verse
problem: Bukhari 4986 narrates the collection and the finding of the last verses of al-Tawba with Abu Khuzayma. The two-witness (written plus memorised) rule is from later sources such as Ibn Abi Dawud and Ibn Hajar (Fath al-Bari 8/437), not stated in this hadith.
old_html: Zayd ibn Thabit accepted a passage only if it was found in writing and confirmed by memorisers (Bukhari 4986)

snippet: Not one Companion accused Uthman of changing the Quran, even though some of them later fought against him politically.
correction: No Companion is reported to have accused Uthman of adding or removing a verse, although Ibn Mas'ud objected to the burning of his own codex and to the choice of Zayd
problem: Ibn Mas'ud objected strongly to the burning of his codex and to Zayd being preferred (reported in Bukhari 4987-4988 context and Ibn Abi Dawud, Masahif). He did not accuse Uthman of changing a verse, but "not one Companion objected" is too strong.
old_html: Not one Companion accused Uthman of changing the Quran, even though some of them later fought against him politically.

snippet: No other ancient scripture has both an unbroken oral chain and dated manuscripts from the generation of its founder.
correction: Few ancient scriptures combine a continuous oral recitation tradition with manuscripts radiocarbon-dated to within decades of the founder.
problem: Universal claim that cannot be verified (Vedic oral tradition, Avesta and other scriptures have oral chains). The Birmingham folios are dated by radiocarbon of the parchment, with a range up to 645 CE, which does not itself date the text as an Uthmanic text.
old_html: No other ancient scripture has both an unbroken oral chain and dated manuscripts from the generation of its founder.

snippet: "There is probably no other book in the world which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."
correction: "There is probably in the world no other book which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."
problem: Muir's words (Life of Mahomet, introduction) are "There is probably in the world no other book which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text." Word order is altered in a quotation. Muir also held that this purity referred to the Uthmanic text and that Muhammad was not the sole source.
old_html: "There is probably no other book in the world which has remained twelve centuries with so pure a text."

snippet: Andrew Rippin , Neal Robinson , H.A.R. Gibb , R.V.C. Bodley , C.C. Torrey , Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri all make similar statements.
correction: Neal Robinson, H.A.R. Gibb, R.V.C. Bodley, C.C. Torrey, Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri make similar statements (check each citation before quoting; Rippin should be removed).
problem: Rippin is a leading sceptic of early Quran history and does not say the text is unaltered. Torrey argued the Quran was fixed by Muhammad himself but had other views on Muhammad's sources. A blanket "all make similar statements" is not supported.
old_html: Andrew Rippin, Neal Robinson, H.A.R. Gibb, R.V.C. Bodley, C.C. Torrey, Denise Masson and Laura Veccia Vaglieri all make similar statements.

snippet: Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, now treat an early fixed text as the starting point.
correction: Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, accept that most of the Quran goes back to Muhammad's lifetime, while still describing a text that developed within his community.
problem: Neuwirth and Sinai accept that the Quran largely goes back to Muhammad's time, but both describe a text that developed (Neuwirth: community-shaped, multi-stage; Sinai: some post-Muhammadan editing). Neither says the text is "unaltered".
old_html: Neuwirth and Sinai, who are mainstream academics, now treat an early fixed text as the starting point.

snippet: scholars who have no stake in defending Islam agree the Quran has not been altered
correction: scholars who have no stake in defending Islam increasingly accept that the Quran text goes back to Muhammad's generation
problem: Overreach: the cited scholars concede early origin and reliability of the consonantal text, not unanimous agreement that nothing changed. Several (Sinai, Neuwirth, Rippin) describe editing or development.
old_html: scholars who have no stake in defending Islam agree the Quran has not been altered

snippet: Each canonical reading needs a mass-transmitted (mutawatir) chain to the Prophet
correction: Each canonical reading needs a sound chain to the Prophet (many scholars require mass transmission), must fit the Uthmanic consonantal outline, and must be correct Arabic.
problem: Ibn al-Jazari's widely used criteria require a sound (sahih) chain, agreement with the Uthmanic outline and Arabic grammar. Mutawatir is the stricter condition held by some scholars (e.g. al-Suyuti discusses both). Stated as settled when it is disputed.
old_html: Each canonical reading needs a mass-transmitted (mutawatir) chain to the Prophet

snippet: both taught by the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari 2419)
correction: The Prophet approved different recitations (the seven ahruf), and the canonical qira'at are held by scholars to preserve authorised recitations; how exactly the ahruf relate to the qira'at is discussed among scholars.
problem: The seven ahruf of Bukhari 2419 and the canonical qira'at are not the same thing in classical scholarship; the exact relation between ahruf and the ten readings is disputed (some say ahruf are not the qira'at at all).
old_html: both taught by the Prophet ﷺ (Bukhari 2419)

snippet: "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold…" Ibn Abbas said he did not know whether it was from the Quran. Ubayy said they thought it was until Surah al-Takathur was revealed (Bukhari 6440)
problem: On sunnah.com, Bukhari 6437 is the Ibn Abbas narration, 6438 has Ubayy's statement and 6440 is Anas. Citing only 6440 is imprecise.
old_html: "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold…" Ibn Abbas said he did not know whether it was from the Quran. Ubayy said they thought it was until Surah al-Takathur was revealed (Bukhari 6440)

snippet: Ibn Mas'ud called al-Fatiha "the seven oft-repeated" and urged reciting the two Mu'awwidhatayn.
correction: Ibn Mas'ud is reported not to have written the two Mu'awwidhatayn in his personal codex (Musnad Ahmad; see Bukhari 4977), and scholars explain this as his view that they were protective prayers or that they needed no writing.
problem: Reports that Ibn Mas'ud did not write the Mu'awwidhatayn in his codex are in Musnad Ahmad and Bukhari 4977 (Ubayy's report) and graded sound; saying he "urged" reciting them needs a cited source. The paragraph handles this with "At most, he did not write", but the first sentence should not imply there is no report.
old_html: Ibn Mas'ud called al-Fatiha "the seven oft-repeated" and urged reciting the two Mu'awwidhatayn.

snippet: Before that, no one in the world, Muslim, Jewish or Christian, could read an Egyptian royal title or funerary text.
correction: Before 1822, nobody could correctly read Egyptian royal titles or funerary texts, although medieval Arabic authors such as Ibn Wahshiyya attempted to decipher hieroglyphs.
problem: Medieval Arabic writers such as Ibn Wahshiyya (Shawq al-Mustaham, 10th century) and Dhul-Nun al-Misri claimed to decipher hieroglyphs, and Coptic speakers retained some knowledge. Their decipherments were largely wrong, but "no one could read" the language is too strong.
old_html: Before that, no one in the world, Muslim, Jewish or Christian, could read an Egyptian royal title or funerary text.

snippet: On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus, the creator-claim of Pharaoh) the Bible actually says the opposite.
correction: On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus), the Bible differs from the Quran.
problem: The Bible does not give a creator-claim of Pharaoh in the Moses story (Ezek 29:3 is a later prophetic oracle). Also, many scholars regard the Hyksos/Joseph identification and the Exodus date as uncertain, so "confirmed by archaeology" is overstated.
old_html: On several of them (Pharaoh's title, the size of the Exodus, the creator-claim of Pharaoh) the Bible actually says the opposite.

snippet: Every detail below was confirmed only after those decipherments.
correction: Several details below have been argued to fit evidence uncovered after those decipherments.
problem: Several of the details listed are not archaeologically confirmed (Joseph's date under the Hyksos, Moses' Ramesside date) and some, such as fired brick, have earlier Egyptian attestation. This is stated as settled.
old_html: Every detail below was confirmed only after those decipherments.

snippet: This matches Egyptian history exactly, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" anachronistically for both.
correction: This fits the Egyptian use of "pharaoh" as a royal title from the New Kingdom, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" for Joseph's ruler. (Many Egyptologists call the biblical usage retrospective.)
problem: Whether the Bible's "Pharaoh" in Genesis is anachronistic is disputed (K. Kitchen argues the title was already used by the narrator's time), and linking Joseph to the Hyksos is a hypothesis. "Exactly" overstates it.
old_html: This matches Egyptian history exactly, while the Bible uses "Pharaoh" anachronistically for both.

snippet: Baked brick was rare in Egypt and appears in the Ramesside period, which is Moses' era.
correction: Baked brick was rare in Egypt, though it is attested in Middle Kingdom Nubian forts and in New Kingdom Thebes, and Petrie found Ramesside examples at Nebesheh. Many place Moses in the Ramesside era, but this is debated.
problem: Fired brick is attested in Egypt before the Ramesside period: in Middle Kingdom Nubian fortresses (Buhen etc.) and in the New Kingdom at Thebes. Petrie's Nebesheh and Defenneh evidence is one example, not the first appearance. The Ramesside date of Moses is also only one of several proposals (an earlier date is argued by others).
old_html: Baked brick was rare in Egypt and appears in the Ramesside period, which is Moses' era.

snippet: in the one era where Egyptology finds it
correction: in an era where Egyptology finds it
problem: Egyptology also finds fired brick in the Middle Kingdom (Nubia) and the New Kingdom (Thebes).
old_html: in the one era where Egyptology finds it

snippet: Petrie's excavations found fired brick introduced in Ramesside times in the Delta, in a tomb bearing a cartouche of Ramesses II.
correction: Petrie found burnt brick in the Ramesside Delta (Nebesheh) in a tomb bearing Ramesside names.
problem: Petrie (Tanis II, 1888) reports burnt brick at Nebesheh and Defenneh in the Delta in the Ramesside era; the "introduced" wording is the argument's, not Petrie's. Could not open the Heidelberg scan to confirm the cartouche detail.
old_html: Petrie's excavations found fired brick introduced in Ramesside times in the Delta, in a tomb bearing a cartouche of Ramesses II.

snippet: In Abraham's Mesopotamia (early 2nd millennium BCE), the leading cosmic gods were Ishtar (Venus), Sin (the moon) and Shamash (the sun), shown together on kudurru boundary stones and seals.
correction: In Mesopotamia from the 3rd millennium onward the Moon-god Sin, Sun-god Shamash and Ishtar (Venus) were prominent, and they appear together on seals and on Kassite kudurru stones (later 2nd millennium BCE).
problem: Kudurru boundary stones are Kassite (c. 1500-1100 BCE), several centuries after the early 2nd millennium BCE date given for Abraham. The Sin, Shamash, Ishtar triad is attested earlier on seals, but the kudurru evidence is later. The order and identification of the Quranic "star" as Venus is a tafsir opinion.
old_html: In Abraham's Mesopotamia (early 2nd millennium BCE), the leading cosmic gods were Ishtar (Venus), Sin (the moon) and Shamash (the sun), shown together on kudurru boundary stones and seals.

snippet: The Quran reflects the actual religion of Abraham's world, which was rediscovered only by modern Assyriology.
correction: The Quran's sequence star, moon, sun is consistent with the astral worship of Mesopotamia and Harran.
problem: The Quran does not name Ishtar, Sin or Shamash, and Abraham's historicity and date are not established by archaeology. "Rediscovered only by modern Assyriology" overlooks that Greek/Jewish/Muslim writers already knew Mesopotamian astral worship (e.g. Sabians of Harran, Ibn Kathir).
old_html: The Quran reflects the actual religion of Abraham's world, which was rediscovered only by modern Assyriology.

snippet: Dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC is "sustainable"
correction: Some scholars regard dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC as sustainable, though many scholars doubt he is a historical figure.
problem: Scholars of the Bible and Near East (e.g. Finkelstein, Van Seters) doubt Abraham's historicity; "sustainable" is a conservative evangelical position, not a consensus.
old_html: Dating Abraham to the beginning of the 2nd millennium BC is "sustainable"

snippet: In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it ", a creator claim with no Egyptian parallel.
correction: In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it", a creator claim.
problem: Egyptian royal ideology did claim the king's control over the Nile's inundation and kings were hymned as creators; "no Egyptian parallel" is unsupported.
old_html: In Ezekiel 29:3 Pharaoh says "My Nile is my own; I made it", a creator claim with no Egyptian parallel.

snippet: The Bible has 600,000 men, about two million people, leaving Egypt, which archaeology cannot find any trace of.
correction: The Bible has 600,000 men leaving Egypt, a number archaeology has found no trace of. The Quran gives no number but quotes Pharaoh describing them as a "small band".
problem: The mainstream view is that there is no archaeological evidence for an exodus of that size. But the Quran gives no number, and its "small band" (26:54) is Pharaoh's description of the Israelites, not a claim about the real number.
old_html: The Bible has 600,000 men, about two million people, leaving Egypt, which archaeology cannot find any trace of.

snippet: But Egyptian shemer means "foreigner/stranger" (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary II p.741), which fits a foreign agitator
correction: The Samiri's identity is debated; some proposals derive it from Hebrew shomer or from an Egyptian term (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary, a dated source).
problem: Budge's Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary (1920) is outdated and this reading of the Samiri name is not supported by modern Egyptology; Egyptian lexica (Erman-Grapow, Wb) do not list this meaning. Other proposals: Hebrew shomer, Samaritan.
old_html: But Egyptian shemer means "foreigner/stranger" (Budge, Hieroglyphic Dictionary II p.741), which fits a foreign agitator

snippet: the name is plausibly an Egyptian title (see Silverstein, JSAI 34)
correction: the name is argued by some to be an Egyptian title (Muhammad Asad, Hamen/Hmn), a view Silverstein rejects in JSAI 34, where he derives the Quranic Haman from the Book of Esther
problem: Adam Silverstein's article "Haman's Transition from Jahiliyya to Islam" (JSAI 34, 2008, 285-308) argues the Quranic Haman has its origin in the biblical Haman of Esther, the opposite of the claim.
old_html: the name is plausibly an Egyptian title (see Silverstein, JSAI 34)

snippet: Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640) : names "the Arabs of Muhammad".
correction: Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640): mentions "the Arabs of Muhammad" (Mhmt, which some read as a title).
problem: Thomas the Presbyter is dated to c. 640 and mentions "tayyaye d-Mhmt"; some scholars read Mhmt as a title, not a name. Doctrina Jacobi does not name Muhammad, only "a prophet"; P2 says all these name him.
old_html: Thomas the Presbyter (c. 640): names "the Arabs of Muhammad".

snippet: Chinese sources : the Tang dynasty's account and Du Huan (750s) describe the prayers, fasting, the ban on wine and the Friday sermon.
correction: Chinese sources: the Tang account and Du Huan (750s) describe the Arab religion, including prayer and a ban on wine (check Hoyland for the exact items).
problem: Du Huan's Jingxingji survives only in fragments quoted in the Tongdian; it does describe the Arab religion, but the claim that it names a "Friday sermon" etc. should be quoted from Hoyland's translation.
old_html: Chinese sources: the Tang dynasty's account and Du Huan (750s) describe the prayers, fasting, the ban on wine and the Friday sermon.

snippet: The Arab-Sassanian coin of Bishapur/Kirman, 66-70 AH, reads "Muhammad is the messenger of God".
correction: The Arab-Sasanian coins of Bishapur (66 AH) and later issues read "Muhammad is the messenger of God" in Pahlavi.
problem: The Arab-Sasanian "Muhammad rasul Allah" coins are usually attributed to Bishapur (66 AH); the Kirman coin is later. Present as approximate.
old_html: The Arab-Sassanian coin of Bishapur/Kirman, 66-70 AH, reads "Muhammad is the messenger of God".

snippet: Sinai's verdict above is now the mainstream view
correction: Sinai's verdict above is now widely held.
problem: Sinai says Muhammad's prophethood as a late-7th-century invention is improbable; "mainstream" is a fair description but revisionist views have not disappeared. Stated more strongly than the source.
old_html: Sinai's verdict above is now the mainstream view

snippet: The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated after 628, while Surah al-Kahf is Meccan (before 622)
correction: The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated c. 629-636, but earlier material, including Jacob of Serugh's Alexander homily (d. 521), already links Alexander to the gate against Gog and Magog.
problem: The Syriac Alexander Legend (c. 629-636) is later than the surah on the Meccan dating, but it draws on earlier Alexander material, especially the homily of Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) which already has Alexander, the gate against Gog and Magog. The argument omits this earlier source.
old_html: The Syriac Alexander Legend is dated after 628, while Surah al-Kahf is Meccan (before 622)

snippet: Genesis Rabbah (38:13, 5th century, Palestine) has a version in which Abraham breaks the idols in his father's shop
correction: Earlier Jewish texts already have Abraham attacking idols (Jubilees 12; Apocalypse of Abraham 1-8); Genesis Rabbah 38:13 (5th century) has the idols broken in his father's shop.
problem: Earlier Jewish texts have Abraham destroying idols: Jubilees 12 (2nd century BCE) has Abraham burn the house of idols, and the Apocalypse of Abraham 1-8 (1st century CE) has Terah's idols broken. Genesis Rabbah is not the earliest parallel; this undermines the point that sources are later.
old_html: Genesis Rabbah (38:13, 5th century, Palestine) has a version in which Abraham breaks the idols in his father's shop

snippet: Jesus and the apostles married (Peter, 1 Cor 9:5)
correction: Peter and other apostles were married (1 Cor 9:5; Mark 1:30)
problem: The New Testament never says Jesus married; 1 Cor 9:5 says Peter and other apostles had wives.
old_html: Jesus and the apostles married (Peter, 1 Cor 9:5)

snippet: Dirham here means a weight of silver ( Lisan al-'Arab : "a dirham of weight"), and payment in weighed silver is attested in Middle Kingdom Egypt.
correction: "Dirham" in 12:20 can be read as a weight of silver (Lisan al-Arab), and silver by weight (the deben) was used in Egyptian payments; critics note that the word dirham comes from Greek drachma.
problem: The Arabic dirham derives from the Greek drachma, so the word itself post-dates Joseph; the answer shows the unit can mean weight but not that the term existed in his time. Silver by weight is attested in Egypt (deben), but Middle Kingdom evidence is thin.
old_html: Dirham here means a weight of silver (Lisan al-'Arab: "a dirham of weight"), and payment in weighed silver is attested in Middle Kingdom Egypt.

snippet: impalement is attested in New Kingdom Egypt
correction: impalement of enemies and criminals is attested in New Kingdom Egypt
problem: Impalement of enemies is attested (Karnak inscription of Merneptah/Ramesses III); say "attested as a punishment" and avoid implying crucifixion.
old_html: impalement is attested in New Kingdom Egypt

snippet: Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir
correction: Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as mutawatir (some scholars read 54:1 as eschatological)
problem: The Kattani classification (Nazm al-mutanathir) lists it as mutawatir; some scholars dispute and some modern writers read 54:1 as eschatological. Gradings by Hudhayfa and Ali chains are not in Bukhari or Muslim.
old_html: Ibn Kathir and al-Kattani class it as <em>mutawatir

snippet: Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE, Library of History 3.44) describes a temple in western Arabia "very holy and exceedingly revered by all Arabians"; Edward Gibbon read it as the Kaaba.
correction: Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 3.44) describes a very holy temple among the Banizomenes of western Arabia; Gibbon read it as the Kaaba, though others dispute the location.
problem: Diodorus places the temple among the Banizomenes on the coast, with uncertain location; Patricia Crone argued it is not Mecca. Gibbon accepted the identification with Mecca, but scholarly consensus is split. The page itself says "use with care".
old_html: Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE, Library of History 3.44) describes a temple in western Arabia "very holy and exceedingly revered by all Arabians"; Edward Gibbon read it as the Kaaba.

snippet: Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which many scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca.
correction: Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which some scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca; others (such as Patricia Crone) doubt it.
problem: The identification of Macoraba with Mecca is disputed (Crone). The word could be South Arabian mikrab, "temple".
old_html: Ptolemy's 2nd-century map lists "Macoraba" in western Arabia, which many scholars (such as Philip Hitti) identify with Mecca.

snippet: The prophecies below meet all four.
correction: Some of the prophecies below meet these four tests; others are weaker and should be used with care.
problem: The prophecies in this section are drawn from hadith, which were transmitted orally and written down later; "recorded before the event" is not demonstrated for all of them (e.g., the Mongols, Hijaz fire).
old_html: The prophecies below meet all four.

snippet: Within a generation all three fell in that order (Musnad Ahmad).
correction: Within a generation all three came under Muslim rule: Yemen in the Prophet's lifetime, then Syria (636) and Persia (637) (Musnad Ahmad).
problem: Yemen accepted Islam in the Prophet's lifetime (c. 10 AH), before Syria (Yarmuk 636) and Persia (Qadisiyya and Mada'in 636-637), so "in that order" is wrong.
old_html: Within a generation all three fell in that order (Musnad Ahmad).

snippet: Heraclius' counter-offensive began in 622 and destroyed the Persian army at Nineveh in 627, within the stated range.
correction: Heraclius' counter-offensive began in 622 and his victories of 622-625 fall within the stated range; the Persian army was finally destroyed at Nineveh in 627, about 12 years after the verses.
problem: If the verses date to about 614-615, the battle of Nineveh in December 627 is about 12 years later, outside "three to nine" (bid'). The Roman victories within the range are Heraclius' campaigns of 622-625 (Issus 622, Armenia/Azerbaijan 624-625).
old_html: Heraclius' counter-offensive began in 622 and destroyed the Persian army at Nineveh in 627, within the stated range.

snippet: Heraclius did, at Nineveh in 627
correction: Heraclius won key victories by 622-625 and at Nineveh in 627
problem: Same chronology problem: Nineveh (627) is outside 3-9 years from c. 615.
old_html: Heraclius did, at Nineveh in 627

snippet: Even sceptical academics accept the prediction and can only dispute its date.
correction: Some sceptical academics read the verses as a prediction of a Roman victory but argue they were edited after the event, and a variant reading of the verbs exists.
problem: Tesei argues the passage was composed after Heraclius' victories (ex eventu), and there is a variant reading (ghalabat/sayughlabun vs ghulibat/sayaghlibun) disputed in the tradition, so "accepting the prediction" is not the only position.
old_html: Even sceptical academics accept the prediction and can only dispute its date.

snippet: Edward Gibbon, no friend of Islam, wrote: "At the time when this prediction is said to have been delivered
correction: Edward Gibbon wrote (Decline and Fall ch. 46) that "at the time when this prediction is said to have been delivered, no prophecy could be more distant from its accomplishment
problem: Quote is accurate (Decline and Fall ch. 46), but Gibbon says the prediction is "said to have been delivered" and is writing ironically; the argument relies on a source that doubts the dating.
old_html: Edward Gibbon, no friend of Islam, wrote: "At the time when this prediction is said to have been delivered

snippet: Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Dhahabi confirmed that its light reached Busra.
correction: Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Dhahabi, who wrote after the event, repeated that its light reached Busra.
problem: Ibn Taymiyya (b. 661), Ibn Kathir (b. 701) and al-Dhahabi (b. 673) were born after the event and are not eyewitnesses; the page also lists Ibn Taymiyya's date as 655 AH while the thesis says 654 AH. The thesis "recorded by eyewitnesses" refers only to Abu Shama and the Medina letters.
old_html: Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Dhahabi confirmed that its light reached Busra.

snippet: Volcanic eruptions in the Hijaz are rare, and Medina has no other recorded historical eruption.
correction: Harrat Rahat has had eruptions in the past few thousand years, but 1256 is its only well-documented historical eruption.
problem: Some scholars note Harrat Rahat has had many eruptions (about 10 in the last 4,500 years) and a possible 641 CE eruption; there are no documented historic eruptions other than 1256, but "rare" is true only on a human timescale.
old_html: Volcanic eruptions in the Hijaz are rare, and Medina has no other recorded historical eruption.

snippet: Abu Dawud 4306 (graded hasan) describes a great city "by a river called the Tigris, with a bridge", called "Basra"
correction: Abu Dawud 4306 (graded hasan by al-Albani) mentions a city on the Tigris with a bridge, named "Basra" in the text, which some commentators identify with Baghdad.
problem: The hadith names the city "Basra", an Iraqi city founded in 14 AH, and the Mongols did not sack Basra. Identifying it as Baghdad (Bab al-Basra) is an interpretation. Al-Albani graded it hasan; Sa'id ibn Jumhan is criticised by some (Bukhari: "fihi nazar").
old_html: Abu Dawud 4306 (graded hasan) describes a great city "by a river called the Tigris, with a bridge", called "Basra"

snippet: In the 7th century, and for 1,300 years after, the Bedouins of Arabia were among the poorest people on earth and lived in tents.
correction: In the 7th century and for centuries after, many Bedouin of Arabia were poor herders who lived in tents.
problem: Arabia included wealthy trading cities (Mecca, Medina, Yemen), and the hadith speaks of shepherds, not all Bedouin. "Among the poorest on earth" is a generalisation.
old_html: In the 7th century, and for 1,300 years after, the Bedouins of Arabia were among the poorest people on earth and lived in tents.

snippet: the Jeddah Tower is under construction
correction: the Jeddah Tower is under construction (check the current status)
problem: As of 2026 the Jeddah Tower's construction status varies (resumed 2023); check before use.
old_html: the Jeddah Tower is under construction

snippet: The word return implies Arabia was once green, which modern palaeoclimatology has confirmed.
correction: The word translated "returns" can imply that Arabia was once green, and palaeoclimatology has found that it was.
problem: In Arabic "ta'ud" (from 'ada) is often used to mean "become" without a prior state, and this reading cannot show the Prophet knew a prior green state. The page's own premise "return" is a linguistic inference.
old_html: The word return implies Arabia was once green, which modern palaeoclimatology has confirmed.

snippet: The Palaeodeserts Project (Michael Petraglia) and earlier work (McClure, 1984) found thousands of ancient lakes and river systems
correction: The Palaeodeserts Project (Michael Petraglia) and earlier work (McClure, 1984) found thousands of ancient lakes and river systems
problem: The Palaeodeserts Project found thousands of palaeolakes (Breeze et al. 2016); McClure's 1984 thesis studied lakes in the Rub' al-Khali. Fine, but "ancient lakes" does not by itself fit the hadith's Hour-related context.
old_html: The Palaeodeserts Project (Michael Petraglia) and earlier work (McClure, 1984) found thousands of ancient lakes and river systems

snippet: Both readings are early; neither is secure enough to build a doctrine on.
correction: Manuscripts divide between "the only-begotten Son" and "the only-begotten God"; most critical editions prefer "God" on the evidence of P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus.
problem: The reading monogenes theos is in P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and is preferred by most critical editions (UBS {B}); huios is in A, C3, the Byzantine tradition and some early fathers. Early support is stronger for theos, which also undercuts the claim that scribes always moved toward a "higher" Christology.
old_html: Both readings are early; neither is secure enough to build a doctrine on.

snippet: the direction of change is always toward higher Christology
correction: the direction of change is often toward higher Christology
problem: Overreach. Ehrman himself documents changes in both directions (e.g. Luke 2:33 "Joseph and his mother" for "his father"; Hebrews 2:9 choris theou; Mark 1:41). Not all variants are Christological. "Always" will be refuted by one counterexample.
old_html: the direction of change is always toward higher Christology

snippet: "Fool and knave, leave the old reading, don't change it!"
correction: "Fool and knave, can't you leave the old reading alone and not alter it!"
problem: The marginal note in Codex Vaticanus (Heb 1:3) is normally quoted: "Fool and knave, can't you leave the old reading alone and not alter it!" (Metzger, Text of the NT). It concerns a scribe's habit, not Christology.
old_html: "Fool and knave, leave the old reading, don't change it!"

snippet: Origen and the second-century fathers read it as making the Word a derived, lesser divinity.
correction: Origen and some second-century apologists (Justin, Tatian, Theophilus) read it as making the Word a derived, subordinate divinity.
problem: Irenaeus, Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria call the Word fully God ("God from God") while subordinating him in order; Origen affirms eternal generation (De Principiis 1.2.9). Only some Logos theologians are fairly described as "lesser". Also Origen is third century, not second.
old_html: Origen and the second-century fathers read it as making the Word a derived, lesser divinity.

snippet: called the Logos "the second god", meaning a created intermediary
correction: called the Logos "the second God" (Questions on Genesis 2.62), a divine intermediary below God
problem: Philo does say "the second God, who is His Logos" (Questions on Genesis 2.62), but "created" is a contested interpretation; Philo also calls the Logos "firstborn" and "image of God" and is not consistent.
old_html: called the Logos "the second god", meaning a created intermediary

snippet: Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Novatian held a "two-stage" Logos theology
correction: Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Novatian are usually read as holding a "two-stage" Logos theology
problem: Accurate for Theophilus, Tatian, Tertullian, Hippolytus. Athenagoras (Plea 10) says the Son was in God "from the beginning" and Origen, Irenaeus (AH 2.30.9) held eternal generation. "Point in time" is not universal.
old_html: Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Novatian held a "two-stage" Logos theology

snippet: In the Septuagint, Exodus 3:14 reads " Ego eimi ho ōn ": "I am the One who is ". The name given to Moses is ho ōn , and the next clause is "tell them ho ōn has sent me". Ego eimi is just the Greek for "I am".
correction: In the Septuagint, Exodus 3:14 reads "Ego eimi ho on" ("I am the One who is"), and the name sent to Moses is ho on. Ego eimi is also used absolutely of God in LXX Isaiah 43:10, which Trinitarians cite for John 8:58.
problem: Omits that ego eimi is used absolutely as a divine self-identification in LXX Isa 41:4, 43:10, 46:4 and Deut 32:39, which is the case Trinitarians rely on for John 8:58. Saying the LXX name is "a different phrase" is also internally strained since Ex 3:14 itself contains ego eimi.
old_html: In the Septuagint, Exodus 3:14 reads "Ego eimi ho ōn": "I am the One who is". The name given to Moses is ho ōn, and the next clause is "tell them ho ōn has sent me". Ego eimi is just the Greek for "I am".

snippet: Several translations render 8:58 "I have been" for this reason.
correction: A few translations render 8:58 "I have been"; NRSV, ESV and NIV keep "I am".
problem: Standard English translations (NRSV, ESV, NIV, NASB) all read "I am"; "I have been" is found only in a few translations (e.g. NWT "I have been", Moffatt-type renderings). John 14:9 has an explicit time phrase, which 8:58 lacks (it has prin Abraham genesthai).
old_html: Several translations render 8:58 "I have been" for this reason.

snippet: The Jews in John also tried to stone him for other statements (10:31)
correction: The Jews in John also tried to stone him in 10:31 and said it was because he "made himself God" (10:33); his reply (10:34-36) appeals to Psalm 82.
problem: John 10:33 states the charge outright: "because you, being a man, make yourself God". The argument cannot use 10:31 to downplay 8:59 without addressing that.
old_html: The Jews in John also tried to stone him for other statements (10:31)

snippet: Thomas' exclamation comes three verses after Jesus calls the Father "my God"
correction: Thomas' exclamation comes eleven verses after Jesus calls the Father "my God"
problem: John 20:17 and 20:28 are eleven verses apart, not three. The same slip is repeated in the Objections.
old_html: Thomas' exclamation comes three verses after Jesus calls the Father "my God"

snippet: the text would contradict itself three verses apart
correction: the text would contradict itself eleven verses apart
problem: Eleven verses (20:17 to 20:28), not three.

snippet: Theodore of Mopsuestia, a major 4th-century bishop
correction: Theodore of Mopsuestia, bishop from 392 to 428
problem: Theodore (c. 350-428) was bishop of Mopsuestia 392-428, so late 4th to early 5th century. His reading of Jn 20:28 is attested (Commentary on John), as is the 553 condemnation of his works.
old_html: Theodore of Mopsuestia, a major 4th-century bishop

snippet: Most scholars read both as status or appearance.
correction: Some scholars read both as status or appearance; others read morphe theou as divine nature.
problem: Contested. Many commentators (Fee, Hawthorne, Hurtado, Bockmuehl) take morphe theou as indicating real divine nature/mode of being; BDAG gives "form, outward appearance". "Most scholars" is not established.
old_html: Most scholars read both as status or appearance.

snippet: Read the hymn against Genesis 3.
correction: Some scholars (Dunn) read the hymn against Genesis 3; others reject an Adam background.
problem: The Adam-Christology reading (Dunn, Murphy-O'Connor) is a minority view among Philippians scholars; N.T. Wright and most commentators see Isaiah 45, 52-53 and Roman imperial language as primary background. Presented as settled.
old_html: Read the hymn against Genesis 3.

snippet: "First and last" in Revelation is tied to being "the firstborn of the dead" (Rev 1:5, 17-18), while the "Almighty" in Revelation 1:8 is distinguished from Jesus in 1:4-5.
correction: "First and last" in Revelation is spoken by the risen Jesus (1:17-18; 22:13), though Isaiah 44:6 gives the same title to YHWH.
problem: Omits that "first and last" is YHWH's title in Isa 44:6 and 48:12, that Rev 22:13 gives Jesus "Alpha and Omega, first and last", and that Rev 1:8 "Alpha and Omega" is used of both the Lord God and Christ (22:12-13).
old_html: "First and last" in Revelation is tied to being "the firstborn of the dead" (Rev 1:5, 17-18), while the "Almighty" in Revelation 1:8 is distinguished from Jesus in 1:4-5.

snippet: Peter walked on water too (Matt 14:29)
correction: Peter walked on water at Jesus' command (Matt 14:29), and Elisha made iron float (2 Kgs 6:6).
problem: Peter walked only at Jesus' command and began to sink; the miracle is by Jesus' power. Moses and Elisha did not walk on water.
old_html: Peter walked on water too (Matt 14:29)

snippet: The Catholic Encyclopedia states that the doctrine of the Trinity is not taught in the Old Testament, and Augustine saw it only as foreshadowed.
correction: The Catholic Encyclopedia says the doctrine of the Trinity is not clearly revealed in the Old Testament, though Augustine and other Fathers read hints of it there.
problem: Augustine found the Trinity in Gen 1:26, the theophanies, Ps 110 and other OT texts (De Trinitate 2-3; City of God 11), more than "foreshadowed". CE also lists OT "adumbrations". Quote the actual CE wording if used.
old_html: The Catholic Encyclopedia states that the doctrine of the Trinity is not taught in the Old Testament, and Augustine saw it only as foreshadowed.

snippet: Jews, the original readers, unanimously reject it.
correction: Rabbinic Judaism has consistently rejected it.
problem: Overstated. Some Jewish mystical texts (Zohar on Deut 6:4, "three that are one") use triadic language, and the earliest Jewish followers of Jesus were Jews. Safer: rabbinic Judaism rejects it.
old_html: Jews, the original readers, unanimously reject it.

snippet: Jews have never read it as teaching three persons.
correction: Rabbinic Judaism has not read it as teaching three persons.
problem: See above; "never" is refuted by Jewish Christians and by Zohar-type readings.
old_html: Jews have never read it as teaching three persons.

snippet: The Bible says God appeared face to face only to Moses
correction: The Bible says God spoke "mouth to mouth" with Moses, unlike other prophets (Num 12:6-8), though Jacob says he saw God "face to face" (Gen 32:30).
problem: Gen 32:30 (Jacob: "I have seen God face to face"), Judg 6:22 (Gideon, "face to face" with the angel), Deut 5:4, Exod 33:11 (Moses). Num 12:6-8 contrasts Moses with prophets, not with all humanity.
old_html: The Bible says God appeared face to face only to Moses

snippet: Laban says " we will give you" (Gen 29:27)
correction: Artaxerxes writes "the letter you sent us" (Ezra 4:18).
problem: Laban speaks for his household; not a royal "we". Ezra 4:18 mixes "us" and "me" in one verse and is Aramaic.
old_html: Laban says "we will give you" (Gen 29:27)

snippet: Herbert Bateman's study reads it as a royal psalm with the human king subordinate to God.
correction: Herbert Bateman argues Psalm 110 is a royal psalm about the Davidic king, though he concludes the NT shows Jesus is also divine Lord.
problem: Bateman (Bibliotheca Sacra 149, 1992) is a Trinitarian who concludes that the NT applies Ps 110:1 to Jesus as Davidic king who is also divine Lord. Using him as support for a non-divine reading misrepresents his conclusion.
old_html: Herbert Bateman's study reads it as a royal psalm with the human king subordinate to God.

snippet: Jewish translations read the verse as "the Wonderful Counsellor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father has called his name Prince of Peace".
correction: Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and the JPS 1985 Tanakh, read the names as describing God: "the Mighty God is planning grace; the Eternal Father, a peaceable ruler".
problem: No translation named. JPS 1917 transliterates the name with this reading in a footnote; the JPS 1985 Tanakh reads "The Mighty God is planning grace; the Eternal Father, a peaceable ruler" and this is the Rashi/Ibn Ezra reading. Name the source.
old_html: Jewish translations read the verse as "the Wonderful Counsellor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father has called his name Prince of Peace".

snippet: ( elei gibborim , Ezek 32:21)
correction: ( eilei gibborim , "chiefs of the mighty", Ezek 32:21, from ayil rather than el, so only a weak parallel)
problem: Ezek 32:21 is eilei gibborim, usually derived from ayil ("chiefs/rams"), not from el ("god"); it is therefore not a clean plural of el gibbor.
old_html: (elei gibborim, Ezek 32:21)

snippet: The verb "sent me" is singular, so "His Spirit" is what the speaker is sent with
correction: The verb "sent" is singular, and some translators (NET, Goldingay) render "sent me with his Spirit"; NRSV and ESV read "sent me and his spirit".
problem: A singular verb does not show that the spirit is not a second object; the plain Hebrew is "sent me and his spirit" (NRSV/ESV), and "with his spirit" is an interpretive reading. Scholar names (Childs, Blenkinsopp, Goldingay) were not verified.
old_html: The verb "sent me" is singular, so "His Spirit" is what the speaker is sent <em>with

snippet: Micah 5:2. "From you, Bethlehem, shall come forth for Me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins ( motsa'otav ) are from of old, from ancient days." An eternal God does not have "origins".
correction: Micah 5:2 can be read as "origins" or "goings forth" from of old.
problem: Motsa'ot also means "goings forth" (KJV/ESV margin), and miqqedem/yemei olam is used of eternity in Mic 5:2 and Hab 1:12. The argument asserts the narrow reading as fact.
old_html: Micah 5:2. "From you, Bethlehem, shall come forth for Me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins (motsa'otav) are from of old, from ancient days." An eternal God does not have "origins".

snippet: Larry Hurtado and most historians conclude that Jesus did not present himself as divine; devotion to him developed after his death.
correction: Larry Hurtado holds that devotion to Jesus as a divine figure arose remarkably early among Jewish followers after Jesus' death, and that most historians doubt Jesus openly claimed to be God.
problem: Hurtado argues devotion to Jesus as a divine figure arose very early among Jewish followers (within years, not slowly), and is cautious on whether Jesus claimed divinity. "Most historians" is unsupported and Hurtado would object to the "developed after his death" framing as implying a late evolution.
old_html: Larry Hurtado and most historians conclude that Jesus did not present himself as divine; devotion to him developed after his death.

snippet: G.L. Prestige showed the early Greek trias was a ranked list (God, His Logos, His Spirit), not three co-equal persons.
correction: G.L. Prestige noted that the early Greek trias was often a ranked list (God, His Logos, His Spirit), while defending the continuity of the later doctrine.
problem: Prestige (God in Patristic Thought, 1936) defended the continuity of patristic Trinitarianism; he noted early subordination but did not conclude the doctrine was non-apostolic.
old_html: G.L. Prestige showed the early Greek trias was a ranked list (God, His Logos, His Spirit), not three co-equal persons.

snippet: 1 Clement 59:4 (c. 96), the earliest Christian writing outside the NT: "that all nations may know that You are God alone , and Jesus Christ is Your Son".
correction: 1 Clement 59:4 (c. 96), among the earliest Christian writings outside the NT: "that all nations may know that You alone are God, and that Jesus Christ is Your servant/child (pais)".
problem: The Greek is pais, "servant/child"; Lightfoot and Lake translate "servant", Holmes "child"; ANF renders "Son" in some editions. The Didache is possibly earlier, so "earliest" is disputed.
old_html: 1 Clement 59:4 (c. 96), the earliest Christian writing outside the NT: "that all nations may know that You are God alone, and Jesus Christ is Your Son".

snippet: Cardinal Newman admitted: "Ignatius may be considered a Patripassian, Justin arianizes, and Hippolytus is a Photinian."
correction: Newman wrote that, judged only by their express statements, "Ignatius may be considered a Patripassian, Justin arianizes, and Hippolytus is a Photinian", and used this to argue the Fathers' words were incomplete, not heretical.
problem: Newman (Essay on Development, ch. 4) writes that if we limit our view of the Fathers to what they expressly state, Ignatius may be considered a Patripassian etc.; he uses this to argue that the Fathers' words are incomplete, not that they were heterodox.
old_html: Cardinal Newman admitted: "Ignatius may be considered a Patripassian, Justin arianizes, and Hippolytus is a Photinian."

snippet: He lists the angels among those Christians "worship and adore" ( 1 Apology 6)
correction: In 1 Apology 6 Justin names the host of good angels in a sentence scholars debate (some read it as angels being honoured, not worshipped).
problem: 1 Apol. 6 is a disputed sentence; the grammar can be read as the host of angels being named but not worshipped, and many scholars so read it.
old_html: He lists the angels among those Christians "worship and adore" (1 Apology 6)

snippet: Irenaeus (c. 180): the Son "received dominion from His Father" ( Against Heresies 3.6.1)
correction: Irenaeus (c. 180) speaks of the Son receiving dominion from the Father, but also says the Word was always with the Father (AH 2.30.9; 4.20.3).
problem: Irenaeus is the strongest counterexample to "begotten at a point in time": he says the Word was "always with the Father" (AH 2.30.9, 4.20.3) and that the Son is not created. Also Irenaeus identifies Wisdom (Prov 8) with the Spirit (AH 4.20.3), contradicting "applied to the Son by nearly all fathers".
old_html: Irenaeus (c. 180): the Son "received dominion from His Father" (Against Heresies 3.6.1)

snippet: Origen (c. 230): "nothing is uncreated but the Father"
correction: Origen (c. 230) taught the Son is subordinate to the Father but eternally begotten (De Principiis 1.2.9).
problem: Origen affirmed eternal generation ("there was never a time when he was not", De Principiis 1.2.9, 4.4.1) and the Son as God. Presenting him as teaching that the Son began at a point in time is wrong; his subordinationism is real.
old_html: Origen (c. 230): "nothing is uncreated but the Father"

snippet: which shows the ordinary Christian was unitarian
correction: which shows that many ordinary Christians were uneasy about speaking of the Father and Son as distinct persons (they leaned towards modalism, not Unitarianism).
problem: The "simple" Tertullian describes were modalist monarchians who believed Christ was God and feared two or three gods; they were not Unitarians who denied Christ's deity.
old_html: which shows the ordinary Christian was unitarian

snippet: Dionysius of Alexandria (c. 260): the Son is "a creature and made
correction: Dionysius of Alexandria (c. 260) wrote in a letter that the Son is "a creature and made", language Athanasius says he later clarified (On the Opinion of Dionysius 4-18).
problem: Athanasius (De Sententia Dionysii) quotes this from Dionysius' letter but argues Dionysius retracted/clarified it (Refutation and Defence). The article omits that.
old_html: Dionysius of Alexandria (c. 260): the Son is "a creature and made

snippet: The Council of Constantinople (381) settled the question, and Emperor Theodosius' edicts made it law, with penalties for dissenters.
correction: The Council of Constantinople (381) confessed the Spirit as "Lord and giver of life... worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son" without calling him "God" in so many words, and Theodosius' edicts enforced that faith.
problem: The 381 creed does not call the Spirit "God" or "homoousios"; it says "Lord, giver of life... worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son". Theodosius' Cunctos populos (380) and later edicts did enforce Nicene Trinitarian faith.
old_html: The Council of Constantinople (381) settled the question, and Emperor Theodosius' edicts made it law, with penalties for dissenters.

snippet: the triadic baptismal formula itself is textually doubtful
correction: the authenticity of the triadic baptismal formula as a saying of Jesus is questioned by some scholars, although every extant manuscript contains it
problem: Every Greek manuscript contains Matt 28:19. The doubt rests on Eusebius' pre-325 citations of a shorter form ("in my name") and on form-critical arguments. "Textually doubtful" overstates.
old_html: the triadic baptismal formula itself is textually doubtful

snippet: and slanders about Mary appear in the same literature (Sanhedrin 106a)
correction: and slanders about Mary appear in the same literature (Shabbat 104b; Sanhedrin 67a)
problem: Sanhedrin 106a is about Balaam. The slander of Mary is usually located at Shabbat 104b and Sanhedrin 67a (ben Stada/Pandera). Sanh. 43a's "Yeshu" is a late passage, and "hanged" is not "crucified".
old_html: and slanders about Mary appear in the same literature (Sanhedrin 106a)

snippet: The boast is real: the Babylonian Talmud has a tradition that "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu" (Sanhedrin 43a)
correction: The Babylonian Talmud has a late tradition that "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu" (Sanhedrin 43a), though scholars debate its date and reliability.
problem: Sanh. 43a says Yeshu was hanged on Passover eve after a forty-day call for defenders; it is a late tradition and does not record a "we killed the Messiah" boast. Scholars (Schafer, Maier) debate whether it is early or about Jesus.
old_html: The boast is real: the Babylonian Talmud has a tradition that "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu" (Sanhedrin 43a)

snippet: The sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke (about 4,500 words) has no passion narrative and no resurrection. John Kloppenborg calls this "the most striking difference" between Q and the Gospels.
correction: The sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke has no passion narrative and no resurrection, though it mentions bearing a cross (Q 14:27) and the killing of prophets.
problem: Q does contain "whoever does not take up his cross" (Q 14:27) and sayings on killed prophets (Q 11:49-51, 13:34-35). Kloppenborg quote could not be verified.
old_html: The sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke (about 4,500 words) has no passion narrative and no resurrection. John Kloppenborg calls this "the most striking difference" between Q and the Gospels.

snippet: The Epistle of James , from Jesus' own brother and the leader of the Jerusalem church, never mentions the cross, the resurrection or atonement.
correction: The Epistle of James, traditionally attributed to Jesus' brother (a point many scholars dispute), never mentions the cross, the resurrection or atonement.
problem: Authorship by James the brother is disputed; many scholars date James to the late 1st-early 2nd century or consider it pseudonymous. Jas 5:6 ("you have condemned and murdered the righteous one") is read by some as an allusion to the passion. James mentions Jesus only twice.
old_html: The Epistle of James, from Jesus' own brother and the leader of the Jerusalem church, never mentions the cross, the resurrection or atonement.

snippet: Scholars from Bultmann to Vermes regard them as written after the fact.
correction: Bultmann and some others regard the detailed predictions as written after the fact; many scholars accept that Jesus expected a violent death.
problem: Not a consensus. Bultmann did; many others (Allison, Dunn, Wright, even Sanders) accept that Jesus expected a violent death. Vermes' view is more nuanced.
old_html: Scholars from Bultmann to Vermes regard them as written after the fact.

snippet: Bart Ehrman notes that Luke removes Mark's "ransom for many" (Mark 10:45) and that the sermons in Acts present Jesus' death as a miscarriage of justice reversed by God, not as an atoning sacrifice.
correction: Bart Ehrman argues that Luke omits Mark's "ransom for many" and that Acts mostly presents the death as a miscarriage of justice, although Acts 8:32-35 and 20:28 are read by others as atonement language.
problem: Ehrman does say this, but Acts 20:28 ("obtained with his own blood"), Acts 8:32-35 (Isaiah 53) and Luke 22:37 point the other way; state as Ehrman's view only.
old_html: Bart Ehrman notes that Luke removes Mark's "ransom for many" (Mark 10:45) and that the sermons in Acts present Jesus' death as a miscarriage of justice reversed by God, not as an atoning sacrifice.

snippet: Paul calls a crucified Christ "a stumbling block to Jews" (1 Cor 1:23), asks the Galatians "who has bewitched you?"
correction: Paul calls a crucified Christ "a stumbling block to Jews" (1 Cor 1:23), though these verses do not say anyone denied the crucifixion.
problem: None of these verses says Paul's opponents denied the crucifixion: 1 Cor 1:23 is about Jewish reaction, Gal 3:1 about the Law, Phil 3:18 about conduct. Presented as evidence of denial in P2, this is overreach.
old_html: Paul calls a crucified Christ "a stumbling block to Jews" (1 Cor 1:23), asks the Galatians "who has bewitched you?"

snippet: Ignatius' opponents appealed to "the archives", the Jewish scriptures
correction: In Philadelphians 8 Ignatius' opponents appealed to "the archives" (the Jewish scriptures), though that dispute is about scriptural authority, not the crucifixion.
problem: In Philad. 8 the dispute concerns the authority of the gospel versus the OT, not denial of the crucifixion; it does not support the claim that these opponents denied it.
old_html: Ignatius' opponents appealed to "the archives", the Jewish scriptures

snippet: The Mandaeans , who revere John the Baptist, deny the crucifixion of Jesus.
correction: The Mandaeans, a later non-Christian group that reveres John the Baptist, reject Jesus as Messiah and some of their texts deny his crucifixion.
problem: Mandaeans are not followers of Jesus; their texts (Ginza, Book of John) are late (post-3rd century, compiled after Islam) and treat Jesus as a false messiah. They are not evidence for the "early period".
old_html: The Mandaeans, who revere John the Baptist, deny the crucifixion of Jesus.

snippet: Basilides (early 2nd century, Alexandria), according to Irenaeus ( Against Heresies 1.24.4)
correction: Basilides (early 2nd century), as reported by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4), though Hippolytus' account differs
problem: Irenaeus' account is not matched in Hippolytus' report of Basilides; scholars doubt Irenaeus describes Basilides himself rather than later followers.
old_html: Basilides (early 2nd century, Alexandria), according to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4)

snippet: Paul's opponents and Ignatius' are first and early-2nd century, the same period as the Gospels themselves.
correction: Paul's opponents are mid-1st century and Ignatius' early 2nd century; the Seth treatise is 3rd century.
problem: The Gospels date c. 70-100; the Gnostic Seth treatise is 3rd century and Basilides c. 120-140.
old_html: Paul's opponents and Ignatius' are first and early-2nd century, the same period as the Gospels themselves.

snippet: Eusebius himself titled a chapter of his Preparation for the Gospel (12.31) "that it will be necessary sometimes to use falsehood as a remedy"
correction: Eusebius titled Praeparatio Evangelica 12.31 "that it will be necessary sometimes to use falsehood as a remedy", in a chapter citing Plato on the "noble lie".
problem: The chapter title is real but the chapter paraphrases Plato's Republic/Laws on the "noble lie"; it is not Eusebius' stated policy about history. Burckhardt's 1853 verdict is also dated.
old_html: Eusebius himself titled a chapter of his Preparation for the Gospel (12.31) "that it will be necessary sometimes to use falsehood as a remedy"

snippet: Louis Feldman's survey found that of 87 scholarly discussions between 1937 and 1980, most doubted the passage in whole or in part.
correction: Louis Feldman's survey of 87 discussions (1937-1980) found only 13 treating the passage as wholly interpolated; most accepted a partly authentic core.
problem: Accurate, but Feldman's breakdown shows only 13 judged it wholly an interpolation, with the majority holding a partial core. Say so.
old_html: Louis Feldman's survey found that of 87 scholarly discussions between 1937 and 1980, most doubted the passage in whole or in part.

snippet: Ehrman accepts it mainly on the "criterion of embarrassment"
correction: Ehrman accepts the crucifixion on several grounds, including Paul, multiple Gospels, Josephus and Tacitus, and the embarrassment of a crucified Messiah.
problem: Ehrman cites multiple attestation (Paul, Mark, John, Josephus, Tacitus), not mainly embarrassment. Treating the criterion as the main ground misrepresents his position.
old_html: Ehrman accepts it mainly on the "criterion of embarrassment"

snippet: Hebrews 5:7. "In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers
correction: Hebrews 5:7: "to Him who was able to save him from death" (Greek ek thanatou, which most commentators take to mean out of death by resurrection).
problem: Greek ek thanatou can mean "out of death", and most commentators read the verse as God saving Jesus out of death by raising him. The argument's "not out of death after dying" is a minority reading.

snippet: Hippolytus ( Against the Jews 9)
correction: Pseudo-Hippolytus ( Against the Jews 9)
problem: Demonstratio adversus Judaeos is attributed to Hippolytus but authorship is doubtful (Pseudo-Hippolytus). Augustine City of God 17.20 is correct.

snippet: yet it is the wicked who expect him to die and God who is said to deliver.
